depth_justification: The copilot referenced some app-specific facts (Google/BNP Paribas buyers, 15-20 person cohorts, the 'aggregated/anonymized' messaging, A/B reuse of session data), but most turns just echo the developer's own disclosures back as near-identical re-identification questions [P3.D2] without advancing, and the final report covered only 3 of the 10 gold dimensions. Worse, it cited MDR Art. 11 and ISO 82304-2:2019 (medical-device frameworks) for an app with explicitly NO medical claims, and GDPR Art. 9(3) for anonymization while missing the obvious Art. 9(2)(a) explicit-consent basis for health/mood data, showing the specificity was often wrong rather than laser-focused.
actionability_justification: Mitigations name relevant techniques (k-anonymity/differential privacy, standalone non-employer consent, plain-language data description) but stay directional with no concrete recipe: no minimum cohort threshold, no parameter values, no UI design, no retention figures. The misapplied regulatory citations (MDR, ISO 82304-2, Art. 9(3)) actively reduce actionability, since a developer following them would pursue the wrong legal frameworks.
salient_examples: Implement k-anonymity or differential privacy techniques to ensure cohort data cannot be re-identified, in line with GDPR Article 9(3) and ISO 82304-2:2019.
Introduce a clear, opt-out mechanism for data sharing and provide a standalone, non-employer-influenced consent form, in line with GDPR Article 6(1)(a) and MDR Article 11.

For instance, what steps are taken to prevent the potential re-identification of users in small cohorts when sharing aggregated mood trends with corporate wellness programs like Google or BNP Paribas? (repeated near-verbatim across multiple turns)
